applied.quote: When you first view a house, ask the agent why the owners are selling, how long it has been listed, whether offers fell through, the age of major systems, past water or insurance claims, and real annual utility, tax, and HOA costs. At the same time, check with your own eyes for ceiling water stains, damp smells, wall or foundation cracks, sloping floors, sticking doors, low water pressure, electrical panel scorch marks, and exterior drainage away from the foundation. Evaluating every property against the exact same points gives you a reliable way to compare homes before you make an offer.
applied.replacement: Ask the agent why the owners are selling and how long the house has been listed. Then ask whether any offers fell through and how old the roof and big systems are. Ask about past water leaks and insurance claims, and what utilities, taxes and any HOA dues cost per year. Check for yourself too: ceiling water stains, damp smells, cracks in walls or the foundation, sloping floors and sticking doors. Run the taps, look at the electrical panel for scorch marks, and see whether the ground outside slopes away from the house. Mark every house on the same list so you can compare them before you make an offer.

applied.why: Breaks up long sentences and removes nominalizations.

applied.quote: The tool on this page lets you create a custom house viewing checklist tailored to the property you plan to tour. Select the home type, the build era, the state, and any local climate risks like freezing winters, hurricane coasts, or wildfire areas. The tool automatically removes irrelevant checks, such as dropping exterior roof checks for condos or lead paint warnings for newer builds, and lets you log answers and issues for up to three houses. applied.quote: Asking why the owners are selling and how long the property has sat on the market reveals whether you have negotiation leverage. Inquiring about previous offers, recent price cuts, or deals that fell apart helps uncover inspection problems that broke previous deals. Knowing the exact age of the roof, heating system, air conditioning unit, and water heater tells you which big replacements you might face first. Inquiries about past basement leaks, burst pipes, and insurance claims are vital, as unaddressed water damage remains one of the most expensive surprises after a purchase.
applied.replacement: Ask why the owners are selling and how long the house has been on the market. A long listing or a rushed sale changes how much room you have to negotiate. Ask about offers, price cuts and any sale that fell through, and why, because a deal often falls apart over an inspection problem. The ages of the roof, heating, air conditioning and water heater tell you which big replacement you would pay for first. Ask about water in the basement, roof leaks, burst pipes and insurance claims too. Water damage is one of the costliest problems to find after you buy.
applied.type: howItWorks paragraph 1 nominalizations and banned word

applied.quote: Checking the physical structure yourself verifies whether the real-world condition matches the seller's claims. When you walk through each room, look closely for water stains on ceilings, around window frames, and under sinks, paying extra attention if someone painted over a single ceiling patch to conceal an active leak. Musty, damp, smoke, or pet smells point to moisture, mold, or odors that are hard to remove. Outside and on the main level, watch for wide, stair-step, or horizontal cracks in the foundation, noticeable floor slopes, and sticking doors that are worth an inspector's opinion. You should also test the shower and sink taps for water pressure, inspect the electrical panel for burn marks or older two-prong outlets, and confirm that gutters and soil slope water away from the building.
applied.replacement: Then check the house yourself to see whether its condition matches what the agent told you. Look for water stains on ceilings, around windows and under sinks. Fresh paint on just one patch of ceiling can be covering a leak. Musty, damp, smoke or pet smells point to moisture, mold or odors that are hard to remove. Watch for sloping floors, doors that stick, and cracks in walls or the foundation. Wide, stair-step or horizontal cracks are worth an inspector's opinion. Run the shower and kitchen tap to check water pressure. Look at the electrical panel and outlets for scorch marks and two-prong outlets, and make sure the ground outside slopes away from the house.
applied.type: howItWorks paragraph 2 asserted intent and long sentences

applied.quote: Property type, build year, and regional weather conditions change what you need to inspect. Condominiums do not require individual roof, basement, or private yard drainage checks, but they demand questions about homeowners association dues, reserve funds, planned special assessments, and hallway upkeep. Older properties require specific environmental questions. If a home was built before 1978, sellers must provide the federal disclosure on lead hazards per the [EPA real estate disclosure rule](https://www.epa.gov/lead/real-estate-disclosure). Homes from that era may also have old wiring, chipping paint, or lead solder, while homes built from 1978 to 1995 often used gray polybutylene plastic supply pipes. In our internal comparison, we saw these rules change the lists completely between a 1965 house in Denver and a modern Miami condo.
applied.replacement: The home type, build year and local conditions change both lists. A condo drops the roof, basement, foundation and drainage checks, and adds the HOA dues question and a check of the hallways and common areas. A house built before 1978, or of unknown age, adds lead items, because sellers of those homes must disclose known lead-based paint under the [EPA real estate disclosure rule](https://www.epa.gov/lead/real-estate-disclosure). Older homes can also have old wiring and lead pipes or solder, and homes built from about 1978 to 1995 often have gray polybutylene supply pipes. In our internal comparison, the same rules gave a 1965 Denver house 12 questions and 14 checks, and a Miami condo built after 2000 11 questions and 7 checks.
applied.why: Aligns condo items with tool rules and softens overstated claim.

applied.quote: Comparing multiple properties works best when you record observations on the identical list during your visits. Use the checklist to mark each item as Good, Unsure, or Problem, and write the agent's exact responses in the "Their answer" boxes. After touring several properties, look at the summary cards to see how many unresolved questions and problems each house accumulated. The tool tallies your marks without assigning arbitrary scores, allowing you to review the specific flaws of each property side by side. Before touring, you can also check your overall budget with the [home affordability calculator](/mortgage/home-affordability-calculator/).
applied.replacement: Mark every house on the same list as you walk through it. Tap Good, Unsure or Problem for each item, and write what the agent says in the "Their answer" boxes under each question. Each house gets a summary card that counts your Good, Unsure and Problem marks, shows how many items you have not marked yet, and lists the first three Problem items. The checklist adds up your own marks and gives no score, so you compare the houses on the Problem items themselves. Before touring, you can check your price range with the [home affordability calculator](/mortgage/home-affordability-calculator/).

applied.quote: A viewing gives you an essential initial impression, but it never substitutes for a professional inspection. applied.quote:
In our internal comparison, we ran the checklist's rules for different property profiles across our 33 item library to test how the questions and physical checks adjust. A buyer who tours a standard single-family house with the build year set to Not sure and freezing winters enabled receives 11 questions to ask the agent and 12 physical checks to perform.

When we ran the rules for a home built in 1965 in Denver, Colorado, the checklist expanded to 12 questions and 14 physical checks. It added questions about obtaining homeowners insurance in wildfire areas and checks for pre-1978 wiring, peeling paint, exposed pipes in exterior walls, and combustible brush near siding. Conversely, running the rules for a condo built after 2000 in Miami, Florida reduced the checklist to 11 questions and 7 checks. It removed basement, roof, foundation, and lead paint checks, while adding HOA assessment questions and hallway maintenance reviews.
applied.replacement:
In our internal comparison, we ran the checklist's rules on three example homes from our 33-item library and counted the items each one keeps. With the default answers (a house, build year Not sure, freezing winters on), the checklist shows 11 questions to ask and 12 things to check.

For a house built in 1965 in Denver, Colorado, the state preset turns on freezing winters and wildfire area. The list grows to 12 questions and 14 checks. It adds the question about getting homeowners insurance, a check for old wiring or pipes, and a check for dry brush or wood piles against the house.

A condo built after 2000 in Miami, Florida keeps 11 questions but only 7 checks. It swaps in the condo versions of the systems and leak questions. It adds the HOA dues question, the homeowners insurance question for the hurricane coast, and a check of hallways and common areas. It drops the basement, foundation, roof, drainage, frozen-pipe and peeling-paint checks, along with the city water or septic question and the lead-paint question. The complete list under the checklist shows the rule behind every item.
applied.why: Corrects Denver additions, removes testing phrasing, and aligns details.
